summary: Describes SIV (Synthetic Initialization Vector), a block cipher mode of operation. It takes a key, a plaintext, and multiple variable-length strings that are authenticated but not encrypted, and produces ciphertext of the same length plus a synthetic initialization vector. Depending on use, it gives deterministic authenticated encryption or protection against misuse of nonces.

eli5.summary: This is a recipe for locking a message with a seal that is made from the message itself, so even if someone reuses a number by mistake, the lock is still safe.

questions: how does siv handle nonce reuse
subtitle: A block cipher mode offering both deterministic encryption and nonce-misuse resistance

tldr.problem: Existing authenticated encryption modes either require careful nonce management with no tolerance for nonce reuse, or are limited to deterministic key wrapping. Applications often struggle to guarantee unique nonces, and key distribution needs deterministic, authenticated encryption.
tldr.mechanism: SIV (Synthetic Initialization Vector) combines a pseudo-random function (S2V, built from CMAC) that produces a synthetic IV from the message and associated data, plus counter-mode encryption. The IV itself is derived from the plaintext, providing both authentication and nonce-misuse resistance.
tldr.outcome: SIV supports both nonce-based authenticated encryption with graceful degradation if nonces are reused, and deterministic key wrapping without a separate wrapping algorithm. It accepts multiple associated-data inputs naturally without length encoding.

today: RFC 5297 is Informational and describes a mode with strong theoretical backing. SIV has seen adoption in protocols requiring nonce-misuse resistance and in applications valuing robustness over peak performance, such as WPA3 key derivation and some TLS implementations.

sections.title: The Problem with Nonce Management
sections.content:
Authenticated encryption schemes like GCM and OCB are fast and secure when used correctly, but they are fragile: they require a unique nonce (a number used once) for every message encrypted with the same key. If an application reuses a nonce accidentally—whether due to a poor random number generator, a virtual machine rollback, or a state reset—the scheme provides no security at all.

In practice, applications rarely control nonce generation: they often rely on a cryptographic library that does not maintain state. An application developer may not enforce the discipline nonces require, especially if the underlying crypto library is not stateful. Key-wrapping applications, such as protecting encryption keys during distribution, need deterministic encryption: the output is always the same for the same input, making nonce management irrelevant.

SIV addresses both problems by deriving the IV from the plaintext and associated data itself. The result is graceful nonce reuse—if a nonce repeats, confidentiality is reduced but authenticity is preserved—and a single mode that serves key wrapping, nonce-based encryption, and key derivation.
sections.eli5: Most locks need a new, unique key number every time. SIV makes a lock where the combination comes from what is being locked, so forgetting your key is not catastrophic.

sections.title: Two Core Operations: S2V and CTR
sections.content:
SIV uses two components working together: S2V (String-To-Vector) and CTR (counter mode).

S2V is a pseudo-random function built from AES in CMAC mode. It takes a key and a vector of strings (the associated data and the plaintext), and outputs a 128-bit synthetic initialization vector. The construction chains CMAC operations together: it starts with CMAC of all zeros (the doubling operation), then processes each string in the vector by doubling and xoring the intermediate results. This novel design lets S2V handle multiple variable-length inputs naturally, without requiring length encoding or concatenation.

CTR mode is standard counter-mode encryption. It takes the synthetic IV as the initial counter value and generates a stream of key blocks by encrypting successive counter values. The plaintext is xored with this stream to produce ciphertext.

The key is split in half: one half for S2V, the other for CTR. This separation ensures that even if counter-mode outputs become partially known, the authentication key is protected.
sections.eli5: S2V is a fingerprint maker: it reads the whole message and creates a unique fingerprint. CTR is a scrambler: it uses that fingerprint as the starting point to scramble the message. Together they make a seal that depends on the message itself.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
To encrypt: S2V takes the key, all associated data (optional), and the plaintext, and produces a synthetic IV. That IV becomes the initial counter for CTR mode. The plaintext is encrypted using the counter stream. The output is the IV (128 bits) concatenated with the ciphertext (same length as plaintext).

To decrypt: The synthetic IV is extracted from the first 128 bits of the received ciphertext. CTR mode uses that IV as the counter to decrypt the rest, recovering the plaintext. Then S2V is run again over the same associated data and recovered plaintext. If the newly computed IV matches the received IV, decryption succeeds and returns the plaintext. If not, decryption returns FAIL, signaling authentication failure.

The RFC specifies three variants based on overall key length: AEAD_AES_SIV_CMAC_256 (with 128-bit AES keys for both S2V and CTR), AEAD_AES_SIV_CMAC_384, and AEAD_AES_SIV_CMAC_512. The ciphertext is always 16 bytes longer than the plaintext due to the prepended IV.
sections.eli5: Encryption stamps a fingerprint on the front, then scrambles the message. Decryption unscrambles it, re-stamps to check the fingerprint, and only opens the box if the stamps match.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use SIV
sections.content:
Nonce-based authenticated encryption: When a component of the associated data is a nonce, SIV provides standard nonce-based AEAD security. The nonce should be at least 128 bits and unique per message-key pair. If nonces are never reused, SIV achieves the same security level as GCM or other authenticated encryption modes. If a nonce is reused, authenticity is preserved but confidentiality is degraded: an attacker learns that the same plaintext was encrypted twice with the same nonce. This graceful degradation is stronger than modes like GCM, which provide no security on nonce reuse.

Deterministic authenticated encryption (key wrapping): When the plaintext is unpredictable (such as a cryptographic key), SIV can be used without a nonce. The IV is computed deterministically from the plaintext and associated data. Encrypting the same key twice always produces the same ciphertext, making SIV suitable as a drop-in replacement for AES-Key-Wrap (RFC 3394) and other key-wrapping schemes. Unlike RFC 3394, SIV supports multiple associated-data inputs and does not require length encoding.
sections.eli5: Use case one: someone sends you locked boxes with a nonce as the combination, and you check the combination each time. Use case two: your safe automatically generates the combination from what is inside it, so you never have to remember one.

sections.title: Security Properties and Performance Trade-offs
sections.content:
SIV is proven secure under the assumption that each key is used for at most 2^48 distinct SIV invocations. This bound comes from the security of CMAC, not from any fundamental weakness in SIV. The S2V function can safely accept at most 126 components of associated data plus the plaintext (127 total) due to security proof constraints.

A key advantage is nonce-misuse resilience: even if an application reuses a nonce, the encryption does not catastrophically fail. Authenticity is preserved. The confidentiality loss on reuse is bounded: reuse of a nonce with the same plaintext and associated data reveals that fact, but not the plaintext itself.

The trade-off is performance. SIV requires two passes over the data: one to compute S2V (the authentication tag), and another to encrypt in counter mode. Schemes like GCM and OCB can encrypt and authenticate in one pass, giving much higher throughput. SIV is suitable for control-plane applications, key management, and scenarios where robustness matters more than peak throughput.

SIV also serves as a pseudo-random function for key derivation, allowing applications to replace separate AEAD, key-wrap, and KDF implementations with a single primitive—attractive for constrained devices.
sections.eli5: SIV is slower than some competitors but safer when mistakes happen. It is like a strong but thick lock versus a thin fast one: fewer problems if used wrong.
